The AP CSP score comes from two places: a 70-question multiple-choice exam in May, and a program you build in class and then write about on exam day. Here is how each part works, when it happens, and what it is worth.

The exam is digital. The end-of-course exam, both the multiple choice and the written responses, is taken in College Board's Bluebook app, and your answers submit on their own when time runs out. The Create task is submitted separately, through the AP Digital Portfolio, two weeks before exam day.

College Board keeps the question types and weights the same every year, so what you practice now is what you will see in May.
All 70 questions have four answer choices, but they are not all the same kind of question:
<thead><tr><th scope=""col"">Question type</th><th scope=""col"">How many</th><th scope=""col"">What it looks like</th></tr></thead>
Single select57Pick the one correct answer.
Single select with a reading passage5Read a short passage about a computing innovation, then answer questions about it.
That is 57 + 5 + 8 = 70. On the multiple-select questions, look for the instruction to choose two. It is easy to miss when you are moving fast.

120 minutes for 70 questions works out to a little over a minute and a half per question. Code-tracing questions take longer than vocabulary questions, so bank time on the quick ones. The multiple-choice pacing strategy goes through how to split the time.

Section II: The Create performance task
The Create task is a program you design and build yourself, on any topic you choose. You get 9 hours of class time to finish three things:
The complete program, which you submit along with a video of it running.
Screenshots of specific parts of your code. You get this back on exam day to answer the written responses, so it has to be readable.
Everything is submitted as final in the AP Digital Portfolio by 11:59 PM Eastern on Friday, April 30, 2027. Your teacher schedules the 9 hours of class time.
• The complete Create task guide, requirement by requirement
• Which code segments to put in your Personalized Project Reference
• Create task rescue kit, if you are behind

On exam day, after the multiple choice, you get 60 minutes to answer 2 questions about your own program. You can see your Personalized Project Reference the whole time. The 2 questions break into 4 prompts, and each prompt comes from one category:
<thead><tr><th scope=""col"">Prompt</th><th scope=""col"">Category</th><th scope=""col"">Be ready to explain</th></tr></thead>
Written Response 1Program design, function and purposeWhat your program is for, what it does, its inputs and outputs, and how you developed and tested it.
Written Response 2(a)Algorithm developmentHow an algorithm in your code works: its conditions, its loops, and what would change if you modified it.
Written Response 2(b)Errors and testingFinding and fixing an error, and choosing inputs and expected outputs that would show your code works.
Written Response 2(c)Data and procedural abstractionHow your list stores data, how you move through it, and how your procedure makes the program easier to manage.
The prompts ask about your code, not code in general, so the best preparation is knowing your own program well enough to explain any part of it.

When is the 2027 AP Computer Science Principles exam?
Friday, May 14, 2027, in Session 1, which is the morning slot. The Create performance task has to be submitted as final by 11:59 PM Eastern on Friday, April 30, 2027.
How many questions are on the AP CSP exam?

70 multiple-choice questions in 120 minutes, then 2 written-response questions in 60 minutes. The 70 are 57 single-select questions, 5 single-select questions with a reading passage, and 8 multiple-select questions where you pick two answers.
Is the AP CSP exam digital?
Yes. The end-of-course exam is fully digital in the Bluebook app, and responses are submitted automatically at the end. The Create task is submitted separately in the AP Digital Portfolio.
How much is the Create task worth?
The Create task and the 2 written responses about it make up Section II, which is 30% of your score. The multiple choice is the other 70%.
Can I see my code during the written responses?
You get your Personalized Project Reference, the code screenshots you submitted with your Create task. That is why it has to be clear and readable, and why choosing what goes in it matters.
Is there a reference sheet on the AP CSP exam?
Yes. The exam reference sheet is available in Bluebook and is also printed and mailed to schools. It explains the pseudocode used in the questions.
Should I take AP CSP or AP CSA?

AP CSP covers the broad ideas of computing and uses pseudocode on the exam. AP CSA is Java programming and goes deeper into writing code. Many students take CSP first. See AP CSA vs AP CSP for the full comparison.

Each AP Networking unit here has two labs. The unit lab is a project that runs across several class periods and ends with the piece of work that unit's performance task asks for. The topic lab is eight checks on a single topic.

All eight run inside the page. The networks, files and servers in them are simulated, so there is nothing to install and nothing real to break. The unit labs say what they need in one line, a browser, and they run on a Chromebook with no admin rights and no networking hardware. In a unit lab you work a terminal where ipconfig, ping, tracert, arp -a, nslookup and speedtest all answer from the simulated network, so the evidence you collect is the same every time you run it.
If a lab counts for a grade, sign in to your class before you start. The labs run either way, but your score saves to your gradebook only when you are signed in.
AP Networking is in its third and final College Board pilot in 2026-27, and it opens to all schools in 2027-28. Pilot schools take the exam on Friday, May 7, 2027.
One device, your own: troubleshoot it, connect it, then secure it. Unit 1 overview
4 class periods. 8 checkpoints. A browser, no equipment.

Four benches are waiting, each with a different fault already in place. On every one you gather evidence, name the layer and the root cause, pick the fix and verify it, then you write the device-recovery walkthrough the Unit 1 performance task asks for.
Open Device Triage Bench

You are handed a device nobody documented, an audit folder, and one setting still exactly the way it came out of the box. The working config files are not the whole story, so you keep looking after the obvious ones have been read.
Goes with topic 1.4, Locking It Down: Securing My Device
Open the topic 1.4 lab
A small office or home network, the kind that runs a school computer lab, and you are the one responsible for it. Unit 2 overview
6 class periods. 8 checkpoints. A browser, no equipment.

You inherit a computer lab network with no documentation, one device that should not be on it, and two devices fighting over the same address. You build the inventory from evidence, sort out the conflict, and finish with the field manual the Unit 2 performance task scores.
Open SOHO Documentation and Handoff
Document a Network From Its Own Records
A studio with no documentation, nine devices and eight leases. Reading the lease table, the ARP table and the inventory tells you which device is missing from the router's table

A network built from a blank floor plan, for a school gaming tournament with a live audience and a livestream. Unit 3 overview
8 class periods. 8 checkpoints. A browser, no equipment.

One switch, and staff, students and guests who must not all reach each other. You assign every port to a segment, decide what may cross between segments, and prove the result with a reachability matrix before you document the design for the Unit 3 performance task.
Open Segmented LAN Build

Finance cannot reach the reporting server. The firewall was changed on Monday and every rule in the list is correct on its own, so you read the rule set the way a firewall does, top to bottom, stopping at the first rule that matches.
Goes with topic 3.5, Controlling the Traffic: Firewalls and Filtering
Open the topic 3.5 lab
The network meets the rest of the internet, seen from the IT desk of a grocery store on a bad Saturday. Unit 4 overview
8 class periods. 8 checkpoints. A browser, no equipment.

A store's point-of-sale system goes down, and nothing between the store and the network team admits to being the problem. You trace the path, read a capture, find where it fails, and write the incident report the Unit 4 performance task calls for.
Open Capture and Trace

A browser terminal, a simulated file server, and a site survey that has to end up on it. The last check is the one people skip: a transfer that printed no error is not proof the file arrived, but listing the folder you sent it to is.
Goes with topic 4.3, Tools of Network Analysts: Using the CLI
Open the topic 4.3 lab

The devices, addresses and command output in the unit labs were written for those labs. Real equipment is messier: timeouts vary, cables fail on and off, and output differs from one operating system to the next. What carries over is the reasoning, and that is the part being graded, here and on the exam. One practical note: tracert is the Windows spelling. On macOS and Linux the command is traceroute.
Scores from the labs land in your class gradebook when students are signed in to your class. Students can work a lab as many times as they like
